title: J-Zero: Co-Evolving a Challenger, a Solver, and a Judge From Zero Data
hook: Self-improvement works when answers can be checked. J-Zero's trick for the unverifiable half: derive the judge's training labels from how each answer was produced, not from the judge's own scores.
key_points: Three roles co-evolve from no seed data: a Challenger that invents harder tasks, a Solver that answers them, and a Judge that scores quality.
Challenger and Solver improve adversarially — harder problems pull the Solver up, which forces the Challenger higher.
The Judge trains on preference pairs whose ordering is known by construction, sidestepping the circularity of a judge grading with its own scores.
Two such construction rules: the Solver's answer beats the Challenger's, and a decomposed-then-recombined answer beats a one-shot answer.
Reported gains average 4.2 points on verifiable domains and 8.0 on unverifiable ones over the baselines.
The authors report improvement continuing through at least ten iterations, where baselines degrade after two.
content_html: Self-improving models work well where answers can be checked automatically — math, code, anything with a verifier. The unverifiable half of the world is harder, because the training signal has to come from a judge, and a judge trained on its own scores can drift with nothing to correct it. Chu, Jeon, and Yang propose J-Zero, which starts from no seed data and co-evolves three roles: a Challenger that invents tasks, a Solver that answers them, and a Judge that ranks answers.
extra_html:
The trick with the Judge

The Judge never learns from its own scores. Instead it trains on preference pairs whose ordering is known in advance from how each response was produced — the Solver's answer is taken to beat the Challenger's, and an answer that was decomposed and recombined is taken to beat a one-shot answer. That gives supervision that is independent of what the Judge currently believes.

Why it matters

The authors report average gains of 4.2 points on verifiable domains and 8.0 on unverifiable ones over their baselines, and — more interesting than the deltas — improvement that continues through at least ten iterations where the baselines degrade after two. Sustained self-improvement, rather than two good rounds followed by collapse, is the claim worth watching. Full details are in the paper.

related.title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
related.hook: Self-evolving models face a dilemma: verifiable environments are narrow, open-ended task generation is unreliable. This uses agent skills as the middle ground.

related.title: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
related.hook: Self-improving agents are leaving the lab for production. This survey, co-authored by Jürgen Schmidhuber, gives the field a shared vocabulary for what an agent can update about itself, and what drives that update.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

flashcards.prompt: Why is self-evolution harder in unverifiable domains than in verifiable ones?
flashcards.back_html: With no checker to say whether an answer is right, the training signal has to come from a judge — and a judge grading with its own scores can drift without anything correcting it.

flashcards.prompt: Where does J-Zero's Judge get the ordering of its preference pairs?

choices.text: From how each response was produced — e.g. the Solver's answer ranks above the Challenger's
From the Judge's own confidence scores on each response
From human annotators labelling a held-out sample each iteration

flashcards.explanation_html: The ordering is known in advance by construction, so the Judge never bootstraps off its own scores.

flashcards.prompt: What do the Challenger and Solver each optimize for?
flashcards.back_html: The Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks; the Solver learns to answer them better. Each one's progress raises the bar for the other.
